source.basis: Operator spec page; structured facts only, no operator prose reproduced.

reading.body:
Only 19 of Texas's 133 mapped data centers publish power figures, and CyrusOne's Carrollton campus, at 45 MW, is the third largest of those that do.

The campus publishes 45 MW of IT load across 600,000 square feet. That is the operator's disclosure, and everything else is arithmetic laid on top of it. At 40 kW per rack, a common AI training density, 45 MW implies roughly 1,100 racks, and at typical hyperscaler utilization that is about 4,400 to 8,800 H100-equivalent accelerators. Those accelerator counts are estimates from assumed densities, not figures CyrusOne publishes.

The 45 MW equals 9.5 percent of the 475 MW of published data center IT load in Texas. That share says as much about disclosure as about size. With the other 114 mapped facilities publishing nothing, the state's real load exceeds the published total by an unknown amount, and any count of Texas capacity built from published figures is a floor. Power is the binding constraint on AI scaling, and this is what the constraint looks like when most of it is invisible.

What the data does not cover: which tenants occupy the space, whether any of them run AI workloads, how much of the 45 MW is actually drawn, or whether the campus will expand. The certifications, PCI DSS, HIPAA, ISO 27001, FISMA, SSAE 16 Type II and TIA-942, qualify the building for regulated workloads generally and are not specific to AI. The suitability score of 71 rests only on published IT capacity and operator type, and it flags announced expansion as missing.

suitability.basis: weighted mean of the published inputs named here, scaled to 100; formula on the methodology page
